summary: Summation No. 34 covers July 1948 and the Ashida coalition's last weeks. The central political event is MacArthur's 22 July letter on National Public Service Law revision, followed by a 31 July cabinet order banning strikes and collective bargaining by government employees. The Diet's 209-day session ended 5 July after passing the budget and a wave of legal reforms: Habeas Corpus, criminal procedure, Reformatory and Juvenile laws, health and medical practice laws, boards of education, and new tax and local finance laws. Party politics show the Social Democratic split, the New Liberal Party, the Nishio indictment and graft inquiries. Economically the report tracks record coke output, the Fukui earthquake (28 June) damage to silk and rayon weaving, price stabilization, rate increases, financial liquidation, trade agreements, nutrition surveys and repatriation. Historians will find detailed statistical tables, legal chronology, labor and press reaction, and war crimes trial results.
highlights: MacArthur's 22 July letter to Prime Minister Ashida held that government employees may not strike; a cabinet order of 31 July banned public-employee strikes and collective bargaining, and wage mediation was suspended.

The second Diet session closed 5 July after 209 days, the longest in Japanese history, enacting 230 of 273 bills including the Habeas Corpus, Reformatory and Juvenile laws and the 1948-49 budget of 414.5 billion yen.
Deputy Prime Minister Nishio resigned 6 July and was tried from 16 July for perjury and failing to report a 500,000-yen contractor donation, while graft inquiries led to arrests of Diet members.
The coalition weakened: a New Liberal Party formed 15 July with 12 members, six Social Democrats were expelled and 10 seceded over the budget, cutting the government margin to nine seats.
On 19 July the Supreme Court, 13 to one, used constitutional review for the first time to exclude a confession obtained after prolonged detention (Imai case).
The 28 June Fukui earthquake damaged 525 of 1,253 silk and rayon mills, and export fabric output was expected to fall by one third; a party of 97 seismologists investigated.
Eight war criminals were sentenced to death in 10 trials, including the Bataan Death March case, while the IMTFE held no session in July.
Land sold to tenants rose to 589,491 cho in June, coke output reached a postwar record of 265,707 tons, and postal, telephone and telegraph rates rose roughly fourfold.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, title pages, table of contents for four parts, and a list of 108 charts, maps and graphs, from industrial production indexes to textbooks, films and SCAP information libraries.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Overview of July 1948: MacArthur's 22 July letter and the 31 July strike ban, the Diet's close with 230 laws, the Fukui earthquake, 1948-49 budget of 414.5 billion yen, CARE, and 45,333 repatriates.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: No change occurred in the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during July 1948. The page also opens Section 2 with its contents list.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: MacArthur's 22 July letter led to a 31 July cabinet order banning public-employee strikes. The Diet closed 5 July after enacting 230 measures; Nishio resigned and was indicted; a New Liberal Party formed 15 July.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: Land sales to tenants rose to 589,491 cho in June; coke output hit a record 265,707 tons; the Fukui earthquake damaged 525 of 1,253 mills. Postal and telephone rates rose and the 414.5 billion yen budget passed.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: The Diet passed a package of health laws; CARE began 19 July with 10-dollar food packages; 1,841,429 people received welfare aid in June. Postcensorship was completed 25 July and 45,333 persons were repatriated.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Government and politics, public safety, and legal affairs. Covers MacArthur's letter, the 209-day Diet session, the Nishio case, 38 killed in Kagoshima landslides, and eight war crimes death sentences.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Politics dominated by MacArthur's letter on public service labor, the Diet's close, the Nishio case, coalition strain, party realignments and graft investigations.

sections.title: Public Service Law Revision
sections.summary: MacArthur's 22 July letter to Ashida said public employees may not strike and called for revising the National Public Service Law. The cabinet issued a 31 July order banning strikes and bargaining; a special Diet session was planned for mid-September.

sections.title: Governmental Activities (Diet, Wage Disputes, Laws, Party Strength)
sections.summary: The 209-day Diet session closed 5 July, enacting 230 of 273 bills. The wage base was 3,790 yen against union demands of 5,200 yen, and mediation halted after MacArthur's letter. The Ministry of Construction began 10 July.

sections.title: Political Developments (Nishio Case, Coalition Weakness)
sections.summary: Nishio resigned 6 July and was tried from 16 July for perjury and failing to report a 500,000-yen contractor donation. Social Democrats threatened to leave the coalition; a poll put Ashida's support at 16 percent.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: The New Liberal Party formed 15 July with 12 members. Six left-wing Social Democrats were expelled and 10 seceded, cutting the government margin to nine seats. Katayama sought dissolution 18 July; a bomb injured Tokuda 19 July.

sections.title: Illegal Transactions Investigation
sections.summary: The Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee pursued graft: Diet members Iimura and Nishimura were arrested or indicted, and Kono, Isazaki and Miura tried for perjury. A subcommittee probed black-market incomes above 5,000,000 yen.

sections.title: Revised Economic Policy
sections.summary: The Economic Rehabilitation Committee's revised program of 14 July moved the five-year plan to 1949-53, aiming to restore 1930-34 per capita real income. The Economic Stabilization Board issued a ten-point draft 17 July.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Floods from 25 July in Fukui, Toyama, Ishikawa and Shiga killed 30 with 22 missing; Kagoshima landslides killed 38. June rail accidents numbered 622. Procurators uncovered about 1,950,000,000 yen of hoarded goods; prison population was 94,700.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The Diet passed Habeas Corpus, Juvenile, Reformatory and Inquest of Prosecution laws. On 19 July the Supreme Court, 13 to one, first used constitutional review to bar a confession. War crimes trials produced eight death sentences.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Thirteen sections on the economy: 589,491 cho of land sold to tenants, 2,711,000 tons of coal, record coke output, earthquake damage to textiles, rate increases, trade agreements, finance and science.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: The Government sold 589,491 cho to tenants in June (1,222,323 cumulative) and bought 209,782 cho. Fertilizer allocations met 70, 59 and 1 percent of requirements; marine production fell to 200,630 tons.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: June log production was 53,364,500 cubic feet. A five-year reforestation program began. July coal output was 2,711,000 tons against a 2,850,000 goal; crude oil was 16,632 kiloliters.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke output hit a postwar record 265,707 tons in June. Pig iron rose 2.4 percent while power shortages cut electric-furnace steel 30 percent. Dyes reached a postwar peak; the Ministry of Construction began 10 July.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Canned food rose to 1,924 tons; wheat flour fell to 26,295 tons; cigarettes rose 11 percent. Pulp reached 39,612 tons and paper 40,555 tons. Watches and clocks set a record 206,226 units.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: The Fukui-Ishikawa earthquake damaged 525 of 1,253 silk and rayon mills. The section also reports cotton, wool, bast fiber and knit goods output, stocks, machinery, and raw cotton and wool imports.

sections.title: Earthquake Damage
sections.summary: The 28 June earthquake destroyed or damaged over a third of weaving capacity, including 547 Fukui mills with 12,904 looms. About 28 percent of bleaching and dyeing capacity lies there; export fabric output expected down one third.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: The Diet passed the Port Regulations, Port Area (418 ports) and Pilot laws. Motor vehicles reached 211,092. Electric generation fell 11 percent to 2,642 million kWh amid drought; gas output was 63.7 million cubic meters.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: The Diet approved roughly fourfold postal, telephone and telegraph rate increases. Telephones in service reached 1,230,872; 6,762,022 radio households were counted. Postal savings restrictions were lifted 20 July; personnel numbered 434,516.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: The Mariners' Employment Security Law passed 3 July. Communications Workers demanded 5,200 yen against the Government's 3,791. Union membership reached 6,629,222 on 31 May; the Supreme Commander's letter halted wage mediation.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Japan signed a trade agreement with the French Union on 6 July, including 25,000 tons of Indo-Chinese anthracite. May imports were $28.3 million, exports $17.8 million; the cumulative 1948 deficit was $219.7 million.

sections.title: Section 10. Price and Distribution
sections.summary: The July staple ration was met in full, imported food being 28.6 percent of requirements. A new price stabilization program raised subsidized basic materials to 110 times 1934-36 levels and repriced four commodity groups.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes outstanding reached 241.4 billion yen on 31 July. The 1948-49 General Account budget was 414.5 billion yen, national debt 367 billion; 20.3 million shares were sold and 47 control organizations closed.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property in custody stood at 65.9 million yen; the SCAP Custody Account reached $286.5 million. SCAP did not object to 766 transactions, 78 firms left the restricted list, and Japan Soda received the first reorganization order.

sections.title: Section 13. Science and Technology
sections.summary: A party of 97 seismologists and engineers investigated the Fukui earthquake. The Science Council of Japan Law (210 members) and new Industrial Science and Technology and Smaller Enterprises Agencies were created; research appropriations were 2,297,500,000 yen.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health and welfare, and education, religion, culture and media: new health laws, CARE, nutrition surveys, boards of education, the textbook monopoly's end and postcensorship from 25 July.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: July 1948 laws: Preventive Vaccination, Venereal Disease Control, Medical Practitioner. June disease and drug output; CARE began 19 July; social security mission report; May nutrition survey (Tokyo 1,961 calories); 45,333 repatriated.

sections.title: Nutrition
sections.summary: The May nutrition survey sampled 42,000 people. Per capita calories were 1,961 in Tokyo, 1,937 in 11 large cities and 2,001 in rural areas. Underweight fell (Tokyo 17.4 percent) but impaired lactation reached 27.8 percent.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Covers the education budget, the boards of education law, the end of the textbook monopoly, religion, cultural resources, the move to postcensorship, and radio, film, theater and SCAP libraries.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: The Ministry of Education received 27,171,630,000 yen; elective boards of education are due in prefectures and major cities by 1 November. Strikes hit 94 of 658 higher schools over tuition increases.

sections.title: Religion
sections.summary: The first postwar Year Book of Religion appeared 15 July; the National Holiday Law cut holidays from twelve to nine. 1,297 foreign missionaries were in Japan; 946 shrines, temples and churches were damaged by the earthquake.

sections.title: Cultural Resources
sections.summary: The Ministry of Education asked governors to help preserve scenic and historic sites. The Fourth Annual Japanese Art Exhibition, set for October and November in Tokyo, passes to the Japan Art Academy.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Postcensorship was extended to all Japanese newspapers and news services by 25 July. Book output was 844 new editions in June. Radio, films, theater, music and SCAP libraries at Shizuoka and Nagasaki are reported.

sections.title: Map of Japan - Topography
sections.summary: Fold-out topographic map of Japan at the end of the volume, with no printed text.
